question: A 28-year-old woman presents with 3 days of pain on right eye movement and progressive blurring of vision in the right eye. Visual acuity is 6/60 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. There is a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) on the right. Fundoscopy shows a swollen right optic disc with a normal left disc. MRI of brain and orbits is ordered. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Papilloedema is almost always bilateral (because raised ICP affects both discs symmetrically). It does NOT cause pain on eye movement, and visual acuity is typically PRESERVED until very late. A unilateral swollen disc with visual loss and pain suggests an intrinsic optic nerve problem.

Correct. The classic triad of optic neuritis: (1) pain on eye movement, (2) acute visual loss in one eye, (3) RAPD. The disc may be swollen (papillitis) or normal-looking (retrobulbar neuritis — 'the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing'). Age, gender, and MRI association with demyelinating lesions (MS) make this highly characteristic.

Incorrect. AION typically occurs in older patients (>50 years) with vascular risk factors. It presents with painless acute visual loss (no pain on eye movement) and an altitudinal field defect. The patient here is 28 years old and has pain on eye movement — AION is far less likely.

answers.text: Branch retinal vein occlusion causing disc swelling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. BRVO causes localised haemorrhages in the territory of the occluded vein, not disc swelling. It does not cause pain on eye movement or a RAPD in this pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: Optic neuritis hallmarks: young patient + pain on eye movement + acute unilateral visual loss + RAPD. Papilloedema = bilateral, painless, late visual loss. AION = older patient, painless, altitudinal loss. These distinctions are high-yield.

Correct. The age, pain on eye movement, unilateral disc swelling + RAPD = optic neuritis until proven otherwise. Order MRI for demyelinating plaques. First episode of optic neuritis in a young woman is MS until proven otherwise.
